porbos.title: Those With No Tribe at Their Backs • That Noon of Scorching Sand • Ahad, Ahad • The Day Abu Bakr (RA) Settled the Price • The Remaining Names • A Father’s Objection, and the Answer from the Heavens • Zinnirah’s Eyes

blocks.0: Those With No Tribe at Their Backs
blocks.1: In the last dars we saw what came down upon the Prophet {{1}} himself. Abuse. Mockery. Thorns on the road. Entrails on his back in prostration. But there is one thing. No one was able to kill him. Why could they not!
blocks.2: There is really only one reason; Allah was protecting him. Allah Himself had told him that He would protect him from people.{{1}}
blocks.3: In the outward view, one form this protection took was the tribe. Banu Hashim stood behind him. Abu Talib was there. The rule of Arabia was simple; if anyone lays a hand on a man, his tribe will demand an accounting for his blood. For one man a whole tribe would raise swords. So Makkah was able to humiliate him, but did not dare to kill him openly.
blocks.4: But the tribe is only a means. The one whom Allah protects, no one can harm, whether or not a tribe stands behind him. Now ask the question the other way round. What would have happened to someone with no tribe behind him!
blocks.7: Those who accepted Islam in Makkah can be divided into three groups. One group, whose tribe was strong. Abu Bakr, ‘Uthman, al-Zubayr (RA). To lay a hand on them meant trouble. Their share was social boycott, humiliation, loss in business.
blocks.8: Another group, whose tribe existed but was weak. Hands were laid on them, but with measure. And the third group. Slaves. Slave-women. Freed slaves. Outsiders who had come from abroad. Those with no one behind them.
blocks.9: What came down upon these had no measure. In Arab society a slave was not a human being; he was property. Like a camel, like a sword, like the furniture of a house. The master could sell him, beat him, even kill him. No one would ask. For if someone kills his own camel, who will ask!
blocks.10: The call of Islam reached these very people. And the most astonishing thing is this; they were the first to answer. Those who had nothing to lose agreed to give everything. And those who had everything could not accept one thing. Because for these no one would come to ask for an accounting of blood.
blocks.11: Has the rule changed! In the office, the boy whose father is influential, no one raises their voice at him. And the boy who has come from the village, who has no place to stay, for whom losing the job means going hungry; anything can be said to him.
blocks.12: In the madrasa, the student whose guardian regularly checks on him is not touched. And the orphan, whom no one comes to visit; anything can be said about him.
blocks.13: At home, the girl whose father’s house is strong is spoken to in a lowered voice. And the one who has no father, no brother, no place to return to; she can be kept silent.
blocks.14: Jahiliyyah has not gone anywhere. The name of the tribe has changed into money, position, identity, the phone list. But the rule is the same. In what tone we speak to whom is decided by who stands behind him. One voice for the rickshaw-puller, another voice for the big boss at the office. Both are human. Why does the tone change! Only the name of the tribe has changed.
blocks.15: The person you can scold most easily today, why are you scolding him! Because he has done wrong, or because no one stands behind him! Let the question stay in your mind.
blocks.16: One more thing. Those whom Allah hears most readily are exactly these people. For the one who has no one behind him, He Himself is behind him.
blocks.18: The noon of Makkah. A noon when one cannot stand barefoot on the ground. The sand so hot that meat is scorched. Exactly that hour was chosen. Umayyah ibn Khalaf would drag out his slave. His name was Bilal. Bilal ibn Rabah. Of Abyssinian descent, a slave bought by Umayyah.
blocks.19: He would be thrown on his back on that burning sand. Then a huge rock would be lifted onto his chest. A rock of such a kind that moving beneath it was out of the question.
blocks.20: Umayyah would say, this is how you will die. If you want to live, disown Muhammad, and worship al-Lat and al-‘Uzza.{{1}}
blocks.21: The scene is like this. Beneath the back, sand like fire. On the chest, the weight of a rock. No room to draw breath. And standing over him, one man; whether the rock stays or is removed is in his hand. All he wants is a single word.
blocks.22: Just say one word and the rock is lifted. Shade is found. Water is found. When we read such events, we read them very easily. Two lines, then the next event.
blocks.23: The man lies on the sand. His back is burning. The rock on his chest is such that the lungs cannot fill with air. The sun is right in his eyes. And the man standing in front says, one word. Just say one word.
blocks.24: If I were on that sand, what would I have said! I know the honest answer myself. And that very answer is the true measure of my faith.
blocks.26: Bilal (RA) did not say that word. What came out of his mouth was one thing only. Ahad. Ahad. One. He is One. The more rocks pressed down, the more that one word. The more blows fell, the more that one word.
blocks.27: He gave no speech. He offered no argument. He did not weep. One word. Again and again. For when a person has nothing else left, what remains is his true wealth. Bilal had nothing in his hands. No house, no tribe, no money, not even his own body was his own. He had only one thing.
blocks.28: That, no one could snatch away. There is something else. He did not say ‘La ilaha illa Allah’ in full. He had no strength to. With a rock on the chest one cannot say a whole sentence.
blocks.29: So whatever he could, that much he said. One word. Ahad. Allah did not ask for the whole sentence. He asked as much as was within his capacity. We often think, if I cannot do it all, there is no point doing it. I cannot memorise the whole Qur’an, so I do not even begin. I cannot keep all my prayers, so I do not take hold of even one.
blocks.30: Bilal (RA) tells us otherwise. Hold fast to whatever you can. Allah knows the rest.
blocks.31: The Day Abu Bakr (RA) Settled the Price
blocks.32: One day Abu Bakr (RA) was passing that way. Seeing the scene, he stopped. He said to Umayyah, do you not fear Allah! How long will you treat this helpless man like this!
blocks.33: Umayyah said, you are the one who ruined him. Now you rescue him. Abu Bakr (RA) said, then sell him to me. Whatever price you want.
blocks.34: Umayyah named a steep price. Abu Bakr (RA) paid it without prolonging the talk. Umayyah thought he had won. A half-dead, broken slave sent off at a high price. Profit in business.
blocks.35: And Abu Bakr (RA) was thinking, I got him cheap. The same deal. Both think they have won. Who won, the whole world knows today. Where the ledger is opened, that is the real matter.
blocks.36: He bought Bilal (RA), and then immediately set him free.{{1}}
blocks.38: Bilal is not alone. Abu Bakr (RA) bought and freed seven persecuted slaves, men and women, in Makkah; four of them women.{{1}}
blocks.39: In a society where women counted for nothing, the names of four slave-women have been written for fourteen hundred years. And the names of those who beat them, no one remembered.
blocks.40: Where is our ledger opened! At month’s end we count the figure of the salary. The land deed, the bank papers, the son’s results; we count it all. And for what will be of use in the Hereafter, there is no ledger at all.
blocks.41: Umayyah counted too. The shiny price that came into his hand, a good deal. Only the ledger was opened in the wrong place.
blocks.43: Let us say a little about some of the seven whom Abu Bakr (RA) freed. Nahdiyah (RA) and her daughter; both were slave-women of a woman of Banu ‘Abd al-Dar. That mistress made them grind flour for her, and would say, by Allah, I will never free you.
blocks.44: One day the word of that oath reached Abu Bakr (RA). He said, break the oath. The mistress said, you are the one who ruined them, you free them. A deal was made. They were freed.
blocks.45: Umm ‘Ubays (RA). A slave-woman of Banu Zuhrah. She too was bought and freed. And ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA). He was a shepherd; he grazed goats. After being freed he grazed the goats of Abu Bakr (RA). Later, on the night of the Hijrah, he would bring milk on the way to the cave of Thawr, and with the flock of goats wipe out the footprints.{{1}}
blocks.46: Just reckon it. The man whom Makkah had kept at the work of grazing goats, on the most important night in history, that same man was wiping out the footprints of the Prophet {{1}}. Whom Allah will put to which task is beyond people’s reckoning.
blocks.47: Hearing these names, a thought comes. All of them were people on the lowest rung of society. A shepherd. A flour-grinding slave-woman. A blacksmith. Today there are exactly such people in our homes or around us.
blocks.48: The one who mops the house. The one who drives a rickshaw. The shop employee. The doorman. We do not know their names. When the need is over, we forget. Yet in Allah’s ledger perhaps his name comes first.
blocks.49: The Prophet {{1}} said, many a person with dishevelled hair, covered in dust, is turned away from doors; yet if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it.{{2}}
blocks.50: This week do one thing. The person whose help you take every day yet whose name you do not know, learn his name. Then call him once by name.
blocks.51: A Father’s Objection, and the Answer from the Heavens
blocks.52: Abu Bakr’s (RA) father, Abu Quhafah, had not yet accepted Islam. Seeing his son’s spending, he was annoyed. He said, son, you are buying only weak slaves. If you are going to spend so much money, buy strong men; they will stand by you, they will protect you.
blocks.53: Abu Bakr’s (RA) answer was a single sentence. He said, I want what I want.{{1}}
blocks.54: The father is reckoning profit. The son is reckoning elsewhere. The father says, buy someone who will be of use to you. The son says, I am buying someone who has nothing to give me.
blocks.55: Right here is the definition of ikhlas. A gift where there is a chance of return is a transaction. A gift where there is no way at all of return, that is giving. The answer came down from the heavens
blocks.57: And the most pious will be kept far away from it, who gives his wealth (in the way of Allah) to attain purification, though no one had done him a favour that required repayment, rather he seeks only the pleasure of his Lord, the Most High. Be assured, such a person will soon be well pleased.{{1}}
blocks.59: The word in the verse is important here. ‘Though no one had done him a favour that required repayment.’ That is, from those whom he bought he had no dues whatsoever. Nor ever would. That very thing became the reason for praise in the verse.
blocks.60: The measure of ikhlas is right here. Allah does not first look at how big the deed is. He first looks at whether a way was open before me to get something from this world in exchange. The more that way is closed, the purer the deed.
blocks.61: Abu Quhafah was saying, buy someone who will be of use in the future. Abu Bakr (RA) chose exactly the opposite kind of people; no tribe, no power, no prospect of ever being of use. The door of getting anything back he kept shut on purpose.
blocks.62: There is one more thing. Abu Quhafah was a polytheist then. He did not understand his son’s deed, nor was he expected to. Yet Abu Bakr (RA) did not get entangled in argument with his father. He ended the talk in a single sentence.
blocks.63: When the people of the house do not understand the work of the din, there are two paths. One, trying to explain by arguing; which often ends in quarrelling. Two, carrying on with the work, and not spoiling the relationship.
blocks.64: He chose the second. And in the end that same father accepted Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah. Now let us look at ourselves. Where do we spend money! We go to the invitation that builds connections. To the son’s wedding of the man who holds power, we send a gift. At the function where our name will be announced, we give a donation.
blocks.65: And the person who will never be able to give anything! We do give him, but the leftover portion. Not the main portion. Abu Bakr (RA) did exactly the opposite. He gave the main portion to people who had nothing to give back.
blocks.66: Ask yourself one question. To whom did I give my last gift! And can that person ever be of any use to me! If the answer is ‘yes’, then perhaps it was not charity.
blocks.67: There is one more point. Abu Bakr (RA) did not merely give money. He made a decision. The decision was, I will stand beside a person by whose side standing brings me no gain.
blocks.68: Many people have money. Not everyone has the decision. Today, with whatever is in my hands, that decision can be made. A phone call. A recommendation. Some time. Going and sitting beside someone once.
blocks.69: The price is not the point. For whom I give, that is the point.
blocks.71: Zinnirah (RA) was a slave-woman. She was beaten so much that her eyesight went. The Quraysh laughed and said, see, al-Lat and al-‘Uzza have taken her eyes.
blocks.72: The blind woman answered. She said, that is false. Al-Lat and al-‘Uzza can neither benefit anyone nor harm anyone. This has come from the heavens; and if my Lord wills, He can return my eyes too.
blocks.73: The next morning her sight returned.{{1}}
blocks.74: The Quraysh said, Muhammad’s magic. Again the same words. When the moon split they say magic. When a blind eye is restored they say magic. For the eye that does not want to see, bringing light before it is no use.
blocks.75: But there is something else. A slave-woman who went blind from being beaten, standing and proving the creed of all Makkah wrong. In her hand there is no power. The argument is there.
blocks.76: And one more point, small but deep. The woman who lost her eyes did not say, give me my eyes back. She said, if my Lord wills, He can return them. Between the two sentences a whole faith stands. One a demand, the other a surrender. She did not demand the eye; she left the asking in Allah’s hands.
blocks.77: The next morning her eyes had come back. Had they not, her words would not have changed one bit. This is exactly where we get stuck in du‘a. We work out an account in our heads; I did this much, now I should get this. Then if we do not get it, we sulk, and give up du‘a.
blocks.78: Zinnirah (RA) was not one to sulk. She did not become truthful because her eyes returned; the truth was bigger to her than her eyes.

footnotes.0: Surah al-Ma’idah, verse 67, final part; ‘wa-Llahu ya‘simuka mina al-nas’, that is, ‘Allah will protect you from people’. Although the verse was revealed in the Madinan period, it is a declaration of the overall protection of the Prophet {{1}}; even in the Makkan period there were several attempts to kill him, and each time they failed. Translation: Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an.
footnotes.1: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–318; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 3/232–234. That Bilal (RA) was the slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf and accepted Islam in the earliest period is universally accepted in the Sirah and Tabaqat works. As for the part ‘he would be laid on his back on hot sand with a heavy rock placed on his chest, yet only one word would be on his lips; Ahad, Ahad’, it is the narration of Sirah Ibn Hisham through Ibn Ishaq; it has no chain from a Companion, so this part is mursal. Acceptable as a scene, not as proof in matters of creed.
footnotes.2: That Abu Bakr (RA) bought with money and freed many persecuted slave men and women, this general point is alluded to in the Qur’an at the end of Surah al-Layl; the details are in Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Tabari, in the tafsir of Surah al-Layl. The incident of buying Bilal (RA) and freeing him at once is narrated through Ibn Ishaq in Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–319; this part is mursal. There is variation in the reports about the price; in one source mention of a monetary price, in another the exchange of a disbelieving slave. In keeping with the allusion of Surah al-Layl, ‘gives his wealth’, the report of buying with money has been adopted here.
footnotes.3: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–320. ‘Abu Bakr (RA) bought and freed seven: Bilal, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Zinnirah, Nahdiyah and her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays, and the slave-woman of Banu Mu’ammil (Lubaynah) (RA)’; this list of names and the number ‘seven’ are the narration of Ibn Hisham; this part is mursal. In other sources there is slight variation in the list of names.
footnotes.4: The persecution of Nahdiyah, her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays and ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA), and the account of their release at the hands of Abu Bakr (RA), appear in Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/319–320 and in Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; this part is mursal. Regarding the role of ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA) at the cave of Thawr, two parts need to be separated. The part ‘when part of the night had passed he would come near the cave with the flock of goats, and they drank milk’ is narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3905, from ‘A’ishah (RA); this has been verified on hadithunlocked.com. And the part ‘he would drive the flock and wipe out the footprints’ is not explicit in that hadith; it is the narration of Sirah Ibn Hisham through Ibn Ishaq, and this part is mursal.
footnotes.5: Sahih Muslim, hadith 2622; from Abu Hurayrah (RA). ‘Rubba ash‘atha aghbara madfu‘in bil-abwab, law aqsama ‘ala Llahi la-abarrahu’; that is, many a person with dishevelled hair, covered in dust, is turned away from doors, yet if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it.
footnotes.6: That Abu Quhafah had still not accepted Islam and later accepted Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah is established by sound chains. And the dialogue, ‘he said to his son, why are you buying the weak slaves; buy strong men, they will protect you; in reply Abu Bakr (RA) said, I want what I want’, is the narration of Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/320, through Ibn Ishaq, and of Tafsir Ibn Kathir (tafsir of Surah al-Layl); this part is mursal.
footnotes.8: In Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an, in the note on Surah al-Layl it is stated: according to some reports these verses were revealed in praise of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA); but the words of the verses are general, so this glad tiding applies to all who acquire this quality. See Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Tabari, Surah al-Layl.
footnotes.9: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/319–320. That Zinnirah (RA) was one of the persecuted and that Abu Bakr (RA) freed her is well known in the Sirah works. And the part ‘she lost her sight from the beatings; the Quraysh said, al-Lat and al-‘Uzza have taken her eyes; she replied, they can neither benefit nor harm; the next day Allah restored her sight’ is the narration of Ibn Hisham; it has no chain from a Companion, so this part is mursal. Acceptable as a scene, not as proof for creed or karamat.

quiz.q: Why could no one kill the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah?
o: Allah was protecting him
The Quraysh held back for fear of Banu Hashim
He always stayed hidden
Bloodshed was forbidden within the precincts of the Ka‘bah
quiz.e: The real protection was Allah’s; He Himself had said that He would protect him from people (Surah al-Ma’idah 67). The tribe was only an outward form of that protection.

quiz.q: According to the dars, what did the degree of persecution depend on?
o: How deep a person’s faith was
Whether he gave da‘wah openly or not
Whether the protection of a tribe stood behind him
How old he was and how strong in body
quiz.e: Where the tribe was strong, boycott and humiliation; where the tribe was weak, beating with measure; where there was no tribe, there was no measure at all. This was the pattern of the persecution.

quiz.q: What question does the dars give for examining in what tone we speak to whom?
o: Has he done wrong, or does he have no one behind him
Exactly how grave is his wrong
Is he higher than me in rank
Will he in the end listen to what I say
quiz.e: One voice for the rickshaw-puller, another voice for the big boss; both are human. The reason the tone changes is itself the real question.

quiz.q: Who was the master of Bilal (RA)?
o: Abu Jahl
al-‘As ibn Wa’il al-Sahmi
Umayyah ibn Khalaf
Umm Anmar
quiz.e: Umayyah ibn Khalaf would throw him on his back on the scorching sand at noon and place a heavy rock on his chest.

quiz.q: With the rock on his chest, which word came to the lips of Bilal (RA)?
o: La ilaha illa Allah
Ahad, Ahad
Allahu akbar
Hasbuna Allah
quiz.e: He had no strength to say the whole sentence; so whatever he could, that much he said. ‘Ahad’ means one; He is One.

quiz.q: What is the dars’s answer to the thought, ‘I cannot do it all, so I will not even begin’?
o: Swap it for an easier deed
Begin only after making full preparation
Hold fast to whatever you can
Begin with the help of others
quiz.e: With a rock on the chest one cannot say the whole kalimah; so one word. Allah did not ask for the whole, He asked for what was within capacity. The rest He knows.

quiz.q: How did Abu Bakr (RA) rescue Bilal (RA)?
o: Secretly took him away
Complained in the assembly of the Quraysh
Went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked for intercession
Bought him for a price and set him free
quiz.e: Abu Bakr (RA) said, sell him to me, whatever price you want. Umayyah named a steep price and he paid it; then he set Bilal (RA) free.

quiz.q: How many persecuted slave men and women did Abu Bakr (RA) buy and free in Makkah?
o: Three
Seven
Five
Nine
quiz.e: Bilal, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Zinnirah, Nahdiyah and her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays, and the slave-woman of Banu Mu’ammil; seven in all. Four of them were women.

quiz.q: What is the significance of four of the seven being women?
o: Women were the most persecuted
Their names remained even in a society that kept no account of women
Buying and freeing male slaves was harder
The price of slave-women was comparatively much lower
quiz.e: The names of those who beat them, no one remembered; and the names of four slave-women have been written for fourteen hundred years.

quiz.q: What work did ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA) do after being freed?
o: Traded in the caravans of the Quraysh
Gave the adhan in the mosque of Makkah
Grazed the goats of Abu Bakr (RA)
Earned his living by ironwork
quiz.e: He was a shepherd. On the night of the Hijrah he brought goat’s milk to the cave of Thawr; this account is in Sahih al-Bukhari.

quiz.q: What does the dars ask us to do about the person whose help we take every day yet whose name we do not know?
o: Give him extra payment
Learn his name and call him by name
Make du‘a for him
Reduce his workload
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, many a dusty person is turned away from doors, yet if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it.

quiz.q: What advice did Abu Quhafah give his son?
o: To buy strong slaves, who would be of use
To stop buying slaves and save the money
To put the money to work in trade and increase it
To come to a settlement with the Quraysh
quiz.e: The father was reckoning profit; the son was reckoning elsewhere. The answer was a single sentence: I want what I want.

quiz.q: In praise of Abu Bakr (RA), verses of which surah are reported to have been revealed?
o: Surah al-‘Ankabut
Surah al-Buruj
Surah al-Layl
Surah al-Nahl
quiz.e: Verses 17–21 of Surah al-Layl. According to the note of Tawdih al-Qur’an the words of the verses are general, so this glad tiding is for all who acquire the quality.

quiz.q: Why did the Qur’an praise the giving of Abu Bakr (RA) in particular?
o: Because he gave a great deal of wealth
Because he gave openly in front of everyone
Because he gave on the direct command of the Prophet ﷺ
Because those to whom he gave had nothing to give back
quiz.e: The words of the verse: ‘though no one had done him a favour that required repayment.’ A gift where there is no way of return is giving; the rest is a transaction.

quiz.q: What was Abu Bakr’s (RA) way when the people of the house did not understand the work of the din?
o: It is good to get into a long argument with reasoning
Carry on with the work, without spoiling the relationship
Hold the work back for a few days
Leave the house and go somewhere else
quiz.e: He ended the talk in one sentence and did not get into argument. And that same father accepted Islam in the end, on the day of the conquest of Makkah.

quiz.q: What is the measure for checking whether one’s gift is truly giving?
o: Whether the one I gave to will ever be of use to me
Whether it was given openly or in secret
Whether the amount was big enough
Whether it is given every month regularly
quiz.e: A gift where there is a chance of return is a transaction. A gift where there is no way of return is giving; the verse of Surah al-Layl says exactly that.

quiz.q: How can the principle of Abu Bakr (RA) be followed even with modest means in hand?
o: Save up and give one big sum at once
Donate to the fund of some institution
Encourage others to give
Stand by someone with a phone call or a recommendation
quiz.e: Many people have money; not everyone has the decision. The price is not the point; for whom I give, that is the point.

quiz.q: What happened in the case of Zinnirah (RA)?
o: She was driven out of Makkah
She was tortured with hot iron
All her wealth was seized
She lost her sight from beatings, and it later returned
quiz.e: The Quraysh said that al-Lat and al-‘Uzza had taken her eyes. She replied, they can neither benefit nor harm. The next day her sight returned.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the condition ‘if He wills’ in the answer of Zinnirah (RA)?
o: It draws the line between faith and demand
It is merely a rule of du‘a
It is a way of avoiding a prophecy
It is just a language of humility
quiz.e: She did not demand her eyes back. She did not become truthful because her eyes returned; she would have been even had they not. In du‘a, this is the very condition we forget.

blocks.0: A Family on That Desert Noon
blocks.1: Now, about one family. Yasir ibn ‘Amir. He had come to Makkah from Yemen to look for his brother. Having come, he stayed. To live there he had to take the protection of Abu Hudhayfah of Banu Makhzum; in Makkah this was the rule for outsiders.
blocks.2: There he married Sumayyah bint Khayyat; one of Abu Hudhayfah’s own slave-women. Their son was ‘Ammar. The whole family accepted Islam. The reckoning is like this. The father, an outsider, no tribe. The mother, a slave-woman, no tribe. The son, a slave-woman’s son, no tribe.
blocks.3: A whole family for whom no one would come to ask for an accounting of blood. The most terrible persecution of Makkah fell to the share of this family. In the harshest sun of noon the three of them would be taken out to the desert. They would be made to wear iron armour and be kept standing in the sun, so that the heat would be doubled.{{1}}
blocks.4: The scene is like this. Father, mother and son; the three standing side by side. No shade on anyone. Each sees the other’s suffering, and can do nothing. One’s own pain can be borne. The pain of one’s own mother before one’s eyes cannot be watched.
blocks.5: ‘Ammar (RA) saw both. His own, and his mother’s. And none of them told another, you give in.
blocks.6: Be Patient, O Family of Yasir
blocks.7: One day the Prophet {{1}} was passing that way. He saw three people standing in the sun. Being beaten. He had no power in his hands then. No army. He himself was not safe.
blocks.8: He did not stop, because he could not stop. But he said one thing as he went. He said, be patient, O family of Yasir. The place promised to you is Paradise.{{1}}
blocks.9: The words are like this. He did not say, I will save you. He did not say, in a few days everything will be all right. He did not say, be patient, you will get the result in this world itself. He said, your place is Paradise.
blocks.10: That is, the end of this hardship is not in this world. He told the plain truth. He gave no false consolation. And this very truth held them. A question comes to many minds here. Why did the Prophet {{1}} not stop it!
blocks.11: The answer is hard, but honest. He could not stop it. He had no state then, no army, no court. He himself, while in prostration, had taken the load of entrails on his back.
blocks.12: When a leader cannot save his follower, what happens inside him cannot be put in words. Yet he did not turn his face away and go. What he could, he gave. One sentence.
blocks.15: One day Abu Jahl came. He abused Sumayyah (RA), said filthy things. The elderly woman answered. He could not bear it. He picked up the spear in his hand and drove it into her body.
blocks.17: The first martyr of Islam. A woman. An old woman. A slave-woman. The first blood shed in the history of this din was not that of a commander. Not of a leader. Not of a rich man.
blocks.18: It was that of an old slave-woman. In the society where she had no worth, in that very society her name was written first of all. And the one who drove the spear, he too will one day lie on the ground. In the field of Badr. Beneath the swords of two boys.
blocks.19: Allah keeps account. Late, but exact. And Yasir (RA)? He too did not survive that persecution. It has come in the Sirah narrations that he died in the midst of that beating.{{1}}
blocks.20: One family gave the din its first two martyrs; husband and wife. And the father’s name remained in that call from the mouth of the Prophet {{1}}; O family of Yasir.
blocks.21: Another thing worth remembering. History usually remembers the names of the victors. Commanders, kings, conquerors. The history of Islam began from the opposite side. The first name is that of one defeated. One who won nothing, who only did not give in.
blocks.22: And this one thing is, in truth, winning. Sumayyah (RA) had no weapon in her hand. No followers. No proclamation. One thing she had; she said no.
blocks.23: The smallest word in the world is the heaviest. Do not stop after hearing of Sumayyah (RA). There are such people around us. There is a mother who has lost her husband. Alone with her children. Society calls her ‘poor thing’, and forgets her when it comes to work.
blocks.24: There is a woman who wants to hold on to the din at home, and the whole family laughs at her. No one stands beside her. Because there is no one behind her.
blocks.25: We have a maid in our house. Do we know her name! Or do we call her by saying ‘hey, listen’! Sumayyah (RA) was also a maid. Someone like her, whose name we take today with respect, perhaps is right in our own house. We do not even call her name properly.
blocks.26: This week at least once, call that person in the house by name. And ask once, how are you.
blocks.28: The father was gone. The mother was gone. ‘Ammar (RA) remained. The persecution on him went on and on. It reached such a stage that it could be borne no more. In the end, what they told him to say, he said with his mouth. Bad words about the Prophet {{1}}, and praise of their gods.
blocks.29: They let him go. But he did not find rest. Weeping, he came to the Prophet {{1}}. Broken down. Thinking, everything is finished. The Prophet {{2}} asked, how did you find your heart!
blocks.30: ‘Ammar (RA) said, full of faith. The Prophet {{1}} said, then if they do it again, you say it again too.{{2}}
blocks.33: Whoever engages in disbelief of Allah after having believed in Him; but not the one who has been compelled to disbelieve while his heart remains firm in faith; rather, the one who has opened his heart to disbelief, upon such people wrath from Allah will descend, and for them a great punishment is prepared.{{1}}
blocks.34: Read the verse once, slowly. Allah did not forgive ‘Ammar (RA). Allah said, you committed no offence at all. In what state had the man come! He was thinking, I have lost everything. Father gone, mother gone, and I could not hold out.
blocks.35: The man who had held on all this time despite beatings broke down after saying one thing. What did the Prophet {{1}} not do! He did not scold. He did not say, you should have been more patient. He did not shame him by citing his mother’s example.
blocks.36: He asked one question only. How did you find your heart! That is, is the inside all right! A broken person is not to be broken further. One has to ask him, how is the inside. In our homes too someone sometimes breaks down. Commits a sin, gives up prayer, goes onto a wrong path. Then when he comes back weeping, what do we do!
blocks.37: That very moment we start a long sermon. Yet the one who has come back weeping of his own accord needs no sermon. He needs one question; how is the inside!
blocks.39: Here is an important issue. There are two words. Rukhsah and ‘azimah. ‘Azimah means choosing the hard path. Rukhsah means accepting the concession given by Allah. ‘Ammar (RA) took the rukhsah. He said it with the mouth, held on in the heart. His mother Sumayyah (RA) took the ‘azimah. She did not say it even with the mouth, she gave her life.
blocks.40: Both are right. The mother is a martyr, the son is not merely forgiven; he is innocent.{{1}}
blocks.41: In this matter we make two mistakes. Some think taking the rukhsah means weakness. So they put themselves through hardship needlessly, and then break down later. And some stretch the limit of the rukhsah very far. Even a slight inconvenience they pass off as ‘I was compelled’.
blocks.42: The condition is this; the rukhsah is only where there is fear for life. Not fear of losing the job. Not fear that people will laugh. Not fear that relatives will be angry. And the biggest condition is the inner one. How is the heart!
blocks.43: One more point is important here. Because Sumayyah (RA) took the ‘azimah, ‘Ammar (RA) did not become smaller. In the din not everyone has been told to walk the highest path. It has been said, know your own capacity.
blocks.44: Whoever can, will take the ‘azimah; Allah will love him. Whoever cannot, will take the rukhsah; Allah will love him too. The danger comes just when someone makes a claim greater than his capacity, and then breaks.
blocks.45: And a greater danger still, when someone measures another’s capacity and blames him. In today’s home this issue is useful every day. At the office one has to write the accounts of interest. We say, if I lose the job what will I eat! A job in a bank. We say, I am doing it out of compulsion. At the wedding function we see everything that goes on, and sit silent. We say, relationships will be spoiled.
blocks.46: The question is not whether a concession exists or not. It exists; Allah Himself gave it in verse 106 of Surah al-Nahl. One who has been compelled while his heart stays firm in faith is excused.
blocks.47: The question is, am I truly compelled, or do I want comfort! In front of ‘Ammar (RA) the alternative was death. What is the alternative in front of me! One more point. ‘Ammar (RA) took the concession, but wept. Even after taking the concession his inside was burning.
blocks.48: We take the concession, and turn the concession into a habit. The inside no longer burns. That not-burning is the real danger. Let me say one more thing. The accounting of the concession is a matter between Allah and the servant.
blocks.49: It is not my responsibility to measure out another’s concession. The brother who works in a bank, I do not know the state inside him. How heavy his burden, to how many doors he went and came back, I do not know.
blocks.50: My job is not to blame him; rather, to try to open a door for him, and to make du‘a. And in my own case to keep the reckoning strict. ‘Azimah for myself, rukhsah for others. We often do exactly the opposite.
blocks.51: The Ironsmith and His Scorched Back
blocks.52: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA). A blacksmith by trade. He would beat iron into swords and sell them in Makkah. He too was a slave; his owner a woman, Umm Anmar. He accepted Islam in the very early days.
blocks.53: What happened then is hard to write. He would be laid on his back on burning coals. A man would press down on his chest with a foot, so that he could not rise.
blocks.54: He would rise only when the fat of his back melted and put out the fire.{{1}}
blocks.55: Umm Anmar did one more thing. Khabbab (RA) was himself a blacksmith; iron would be heated in his own furnace, then that hot iron would be pressed on his head.
blocks.56: To burn him with the tool of his own hand. One wonders how cruel a person can be. And one wonders even more how much a person can endure.
blocks.57: Khabbab (RA) could have run away if he wished. He could have left Makkah. He did not. Because the thing he had found was not something to leave. People endure hardship for two reasons. Either there is no way to flee. Or what they have gained is greater than the hardship.
blocks.58: In their case, the second. In our case, which! The prayer we pray out of habit, the fast we keep because everyone keeps it; those, for what reason! In front of Khabbab (RA) the way of escape was wide open.
blocks.59: He did not go, because the thing was precious to him. The day the din truly feels precious, the thought of giving it up will no longer come to mind.
blocks.60: The Reckoning of al-‘As ibn Wa’il
blocks.61: Khabbab (RA) had a debt owed to him by al-‘As ibn Wa’il. He had done blacksmith’s work for him, the money was outstanding. He went to ask for the money. Al-‘As said, I will not pay the money until you deny Muhammad.
blocks.62: Khabbab (RA) replied, even if you die and come back to life, I will not deny him. Al-‘As then said with a laugh, all right. If after death I really am brought to life, then there too I will have plenty of wealth and children. I will pay your due then.{{1}}
blocks.63: The words were said in mockery. But Allah held on to the mockery
blocks.65: Have you seen the one who rejects Our verses and says, (in the Hereafter too) I shall surely be given wealth and children. Has he then peeped into the unseen, or has he taken a promise from the Most Merciful Allah? Never. Whatever he says, I will write that down too, and increase his punishment. And of what he speaks of (that is, that wealth and those children), I will be the heir. And he will come to Me alone.{{1}}
blocks.66: A poor blacksmith did not get his money owed. And his word found its way into the Qur’an. For fourteen hundred years millions of people have been reading it. The one who withheld the money, his name too remained; but how!
blocks.67: There is something else. What did al-‘As ibn Wa’il actually think! He thought, if there is anything in the Hereafter too, there too I will be rich. This thought has not died. Even today many think, whoever has everything in this world will have everything in the Hereafter too. Surely Allah loves him, otherwise why would He give so much!
blocks.68: The Qur’an has broken this reckoning. Worldly wealth is not proof of love. It is an instrument of testing. And the last word of the verse is frighteningly beautiful. ‘And he will come to Me alone.’ The one who boasted of wealth and children, on that day no one will be beside him.

footnotes.0: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–318; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. That ‘Ammar ibn Yasir (RA) was a Companion and his standing are established by sound chains. As for the account, ‘Yasir ibn ‘Amir came to Makkah from Yemen in search of his brother and stayed, lived under the protection of Banu Makhzum; he married Sumayyah bint Khayyat; the whole family was tortured by being made to stand in the desert in the noon sun’, this part is the narration of the Sirah and Tabaqat works; this part is mursal.
footnotes.1: ‘Sabran, ala ali Yasir, fa-inna maw‘idakumu al-jannah’; be patient, O family of Yasir, your promised place is Paradise. The sentence is narrated in Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; al-Bayhaqi, Dala’il al-Nubuwwah. Al-Hakim called it sahih, but this assessment of his is open to discussion; many have called the chain mursal or weak. That is, this full sentence itself falls within that discussion. In the dars it is used as a scene of consolation; no ruling or point of creed has been built upon it.
footnotes.2: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/318; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 8/264. That Sumayyah (RA) is the first martyr of Islam is universally accepted in the Sirah, Tabaqat and history works. As for the specific account, ‘Abu Jahl struck her with a spear, and she was martyred there’, it is the narration of Ibn Hisham and Ibn Sa‘d; it has no chain from a Companion, so this part is mursal.
footnotes.3: That Yasir (RA) died as a result of the persecution is narrated in the Sirah and Tabaqat works (Ibn Ishaq; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra); in some narrations it has come that Abu Jahl killed him too. The account is of the Sirah; the chain is mursal. The history books agree that Sumayyah (RA) is the first martyr of Islam.
footnotes.4: The ruling of verse 106 of Surah al-Nahl is definitive; the verse is part of the Qur’an. As for the account of the occasion of revelation, “‘Ammar (RA), compelled by the persecution, said what they demanded, then came weeping to the Prophet {{1}}; the Prophet {{2}} asked, how did you find your heart; he said, steadfast in faith; the Prophet {{3}} said, if they do it again, say it again”, it is narrated in Ibn Ishaq; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; al-Bayhaqi; Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Tabari (Surah al-Nahl 106). Although well known in the books of tafsir and Sirah, there is discussion about the chain; some have called it mursal. That is, the ruling of the verse is certain, while this account of the incident is report-based.
footnotes.6: Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an, note on Surah al-Nahl 106: if fear for life arises for someone, and he is threatened that he will be killed if he does not utter words of disbelief, then he is excused (ma‘dhur); if he utters them he is forgivable. The condition is that his heart must stay firm in faith. But if someone speaks words of disbelief willingly and knowingly, the wrath of Allah will descend upon him. This is the dividing line between rukhsah and ‘azimah.
footnotes.7: That Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA) was a blacksmith and one of the persecuted Companions has come in several hadiths of Sahih al-Bukhari; see hadith 2091 and 3612. As for the specific account, ‘his owner was Umm Anmar; she would bring hot iron and press it on his back, and the fat of his back would melt and put out the fire’, it is the narration of Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham and Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 3/116–117; this part is mursal.
footnotes.8: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 2091, 2275 and 4732; from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA). Verified on hadithunlocked.com (bukhari:2091). Concerning the demand for his dues from al-‘As ibn Wa’il, his mockery, and the revelation of verse 77 of Surah Maryam. The incident is also given in detail in Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an in the note on Surah Maryam 77.

quiz.q: Where had Yasir (RA) come to Makkah from, and why?
o: From Yemen, to look for his brother
From Abyssinia, for trade
From Ta’if, to take refuge
From Madinah, to relatives
quiz.e: Having come from Yemen to look for his brother, he stayed. As an outsider he had to live under the protection of Banu Makhzum; so he had no protection of a tribe.

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ say only a single sentence to the family of Yasir, without stopping it?
o: There was no time
He wanted to prolong the test
They had not asked for help
He did not then have the power to stop it
quiz.e: Then there was no state, no army, no court; he himself was not safe. What he could, he gave. Sometimes one sentence is everything.

quiz.q: What was the end of Yasir (RA)?
o: After some time he left Makkah and returned to Yemen
He died in the midst of the persecution
He migrated to Abyssinia
The Quraysh finally released him
quiz.e: It has come in the Sirah narrations that, like Sumayyah (RA), Yasir (RA) too did not survive that persecution; one family gave the din its first two martyrs.

quiz.q: Who is the first martyr of Islam?
o: Yasir ibn ‘Amir (RA)
‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA)
Khabbab (RA)
Sumayyah (RA)
quiz.e: She was martyred by the spear of Abu Jahl. The first blood shed in the history of this din is not that of a commander; it is that of an old slave-woman.

quiz.q: Which verse was revealed in the incident of ‘Ammar (RA)?
o: Surah Maryam, verse 77
Surah al-Nahl, verse 106
Surah al-Buruj, verse 8
Surah al-Layl, verse 17
quiz.e: The verse says: one who has been compelled while his heart is firm in faith does not fall under it. Allah did not forgive; He said there was no offence at all.

quiz.q: What lesson is there in the Prophet ﷺ asking ‘Ammar (RA) a question instead of scolding him?
o: Pointing out the mistake is not at all necessary
A broken person must be asked after his inner state
Asking a question brings the truth out
Silence is the best answer
quiz.e: The one who has come back weeping of his own accord needs no sermon. When someone at home comes back broken, we start a long sermon at once.

quiz.q: According to the dars, what should be done when someone at home comes back weeping after sinning?
o: Explain in detail where the mistake happened
Keep him at a distance for some days
Have an elder tell him
Ask how his inside is
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ did not scold ‘Ammar (RA), did not shame him, did not cite his mother’s example. He asked one question only: how did you find your heart!

quiz.q: What does the word ‘azimah mean?
o: Accepting the concession given by Allah
Carrying on the deed in secret
Moving away from danger
Choosing the hard path
quiz.e: Sumayyah (RA) took the ‘azimah, and gave her life. ‘Ammar (RA) took the rukhsah, and held on to his heart. Both are right.

quiz.q: According to Tawdih al-Qur’an, which is the main condition of the rukhsah?
o: Repenting afterward is enough
The heart staying firm in faith
Keeping a few witnesses
Taking the permission of a scholar
quiz.e: If fear for life arises and one is compelled to utter words of disbelief, he is excused; the condition is that the heart stays firm in faith. If said willingly, wrath.

quiz.q: How were both right, though the mother took the ‘azimah and the son the rukhsah?
o: Everyone has not been told to take the highest path
The circumstances of the two were not at all alike
The son was very young then
The mother had accepted Islam earlier
quiz.e: Whoever can takes the ‘azimah, whoever cannot takes the rukhsah. The danger is making a claim bigger than one’s own capacity and breaking, and measuring another’s capacity and blaming him.

quiz.q: Before saying ‘I am doing it out of compulsion’, which question must one ask oneself?
o: What are others doing in this situation
Am I truly compelled, or do I want comfort
How long will this situation go on
Whether anyone is seeing me here
quiz.e: In front of ‘Ammar (RA) the alternative was death. The rukhsah is only where there is fear for life; not fear of the job or of public shame.

quiz.q: What should my stance be about another’s rukhsah and ‘azimah?
o: Not blame him without knowing his inner state
Correct him openly in front of everyone
Reduce mixing with him
Complain about the matter to a scholar
quiz.e: How heavy his burden, to how many doors he went and came back, I do not know. ‘Azimah for myself, rukhsah for others; we often do the opposite.

quiz.q: What was the profession of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA)?
o: Blacksmith
Shepherd
Merchant
Weaver
quiz.e: He would beat iron into swords. Iron was heated in his own furnace, and that same hot iron was pressed on his head.

quiz.q: Khabbab (RA) could have fled; why did he not?
o: No way of escape was open at all
The Prophet ﷺ had forbidden him to leave Makkah
What he had found was greater than the hardship
His whole family was in Makkah
quiz.e: People endure hardship for two reasons; either there is no way to flee, or what they have gained is greater than the hardship. In their case, the second.

quiz.q: What condition did al-‘As ibn Wa’il set for paying Khabbab’s (RA) dues?
o: To leave Makkah for ever
To worship al-Lat and al-‘Uzza
To deny Muhammad ﷺ
To do the work again afresh
quiz.e: Khabbab (RA) replied, even if you die and come to life again I will not deny him. He then said mockingly, there too I will have wealth and children.

quiz.q: Which verses were revealed in reply to al-‘As ibn Wa’il’s mockery?
o: Surah Maryam 77–80
Surah al-‘Ankabut, verses 1–3
Surah al-Layl 17–21
Surah al-Buruj 4–8
quiz.e: The verses were revealed in the context of this incident narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari. The word of the last verse is frightening: ‘And he will come to Me alone’.

quiz.q: How does the Qur’an break the notion that ‘whoever has everything in this world has everything in the Hereafter too’?
o: By saying wealth is not proof of love but a test
By forbidding the keeping of wealth altogether
By announcing punishment for all rich people
By declaring poverty the best state
quiz.e: The thought of al-‘As ibn Wa’il has not died even today. The last word of the verse: ‘And he will come to Me alone’; neither wealth nor children will be with him.

blocks.0: That Question in the Shade of the Ka‘bah
blocks.1: One day Khabbab (RA) and several Companions came to the Prophet {{1}}. He was sitting in the shade of the Ka‘bah. He had made his cloak a pillow and was reclining. That scene. A cloak. The shade of a wall. And a group of men whose bodies were full of wounds.
blocks.2: Khabbab (RA) said, will you not ask for help for us! Will you not make du‘a for us! The Prophet {{1}} sat up. His face turned red.
blocks.3: He said, among those before you there was a man who would be seized, a hole dug for him in the ground, and he would be placed in it. Then a saw would be brought and placed on his head, and he would be split in two. Yet he did not turn from his din. His flesh would be stripped from his bones with iron combs. Yet he did not turn from his din.
blocks.4: Then he said, by Allah, Allah will surely complete this matter. A day will come when a rider will travel alone from San‘a to Hadramawt, with no fear in his heart of anyone but Allah; at most the fear of a wolf for his goats.
blocks.5: At the end he said, but you are in a hurry.{{1}}
blocks.6: He did not make du‘a. The one at whose du‘a rain would fall from the sky, did not make du‘a for these men. Why! Because this hardship had a work to do.
blocks.7: He had been angry. His face had turned red. Angry at whom! Not at Khabbab (RA). The anger was at an idea inside the question. The idea was this; if you follow the din, there will be no hardship.
blocks.8: He broke that very idea. He said, there were people before you too; they were cut in two with saws. That is, there is hardship on this path. There was, and there will be. But at the same moment he said another thing. This will end.
blocks.9: Two things together. Hardship will remain, and victory will surely come. We often take one and drop the other. One speaks only of hardship; people become despondent. One speaks only of victory; people go in without preparation, then break down at the first blow.
blocks.10: The Prophet {{1}} said both, in the same breath. ‘But you are in a hurry.’ The words touch us too. We make du‘a, and sit watching the clock. A week. A month. A year. Then we say, it did not happen.
blocks.11: We think du‘a is a button; press it and the thing is done. What Khabbab (RA) asked for that day, he got. But not at once. He lived. He saw the conquest of Makkah. He saw the fall of Rome and Persia. He lived to see that rider able to go alone from San‘a to Hadramawt.
blocks.12: It only took time. Allah’s clock does not match our clock. On our clock thirteen years is a large part of a life. By Allah’s reckoning thirteen years is the time of laying a foundation.
blocks.13: A foundation laid in haste, nothing stands on it. What is haste, really! Haste means not accepting Allah’s timetable. I decide when the thing should happen. Then if it does not happen on that date, I assume it will not.
blocks.14: Yet I do not know when the thing is good to happen. I do not know whether getting it today would have been good for me, or harm. A small example. If the child asks today and the father gives tomorrow, the boy thinks, father did not give. The father knows that giving it today would have harmed the boy.
blocks.15: We are that boy. The difference is, the father’s knowledge is limited; and the One we are asking has infinite knowledge.
blocks.16: The Day ‘Umar (RA) Was Shown the Back
blocks.17: This is from many years later. ‘Umar (RA) was then the caliph. The capital of Islam, Madinah. Rome and Persia had both collapsed. One day Khabbab (RA) came to him.
blocks.18: ‘Umar (RA) seated him in his own seat. He said, in this world only one man had more right to this seat; Bilal. Khabbab (RA) said, why, Amir al-Mu’minin!
blocks.19: Then in the course of talk he uncovered his back and showed it. ‘Umar (RA) kept looking. He said, I have never seen a back like this. Khabbab (RA) said, I used to be laid on the fire. That fire would not go out until the fat of my back melted and flowed down.{{1}}
blocks.20: There is something here. Year after year has passed. Islam has won. But the mark has not gone. Those who won, the price of winning was written on their bodies. We have received the state of having won. We have not paid the price.
blocks.21: Did We Get Our Reward in This World Itself
blocks.22: In his last years Khabbab (RA) became well off. A house, wealth. And seeing it he would weep. He would say, we migrated with the Prophet {{1}} only for the pleasure of Allah. Our reward with Allah had become fixed.
blocks.23: Then he would speak of Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA). He was martyred on the day of Uhud. There was only one cloak to shroud him. If the head was covered, the feet came out. If the feet were covered, the head came out.
blocks.24: The Prophet {{1}} said, cover the head, and put idhkhir grass over the feet. Khabbab (RA) would say, some of us have gone, without enjoying any of their fruit in this world. And the fruit of some of us has ripened; he is now gathering it.{{2}}
blocks.25: A fear lies hidden inside those words. He was afraid, was my reward given to me in this world itself! We fear exactly the opposite. We fear, why did I get nothing in this world. He feared, why did I get in this world.
blocks.26: The whole difference lies between these two fears. Here one thing needs to be made clear. Being well off in this world is not a fault. Having wealth is not a fault. Khabbab (RA) did not throw wealth away. He was only afraid, lest the account be settled here.
blocks.27: This fear is what keeps a believer moving. The one who has nothing thinks; Allah has forgotten me. The one who has everything thinks; Allah loves me. Both are wrong reckonings.
blocks.28: Wealth is one form of test, want is also one form of test. The question is not what I got; the question is what I did with what I got.
blocks.30: Let me name one more. Suhayb ibn Sinan (RA). He had lived as a captive in Rome, then came to Makkah, and built wealth through trade. Everyone knew him by the name ‘Suhayb al-Rumi’.
blocks.31: He too accepted Islam. Persecution came down on him too; because he too had no tribe. Later at the time of the Hijrah, when he took the road to Madinah, the Quraysh stood blocking the way.
blocks.32: They said, you came penniless, you built wealth here with us. Now you will take it all and go! That will not happen. He said, well, if I give you all my wealth, will you clear the way!
blocks.33: They said, we will. He gave everything. He began walking toward Madinah empty-handed. When he reached Madinah, the Prophet {{1}} saw him and said, the deal was profitable, O Abu Yahya! The deal was profitable!{{2}}
blocks.34: The savings of a whole life gone in a moment. And he walked on with a smile. Because the one who knows what he is buying does not haggle over the price.
blocks.35: The Day Abu Dharr Stood Before the Ka‘bah
blocks.36: Let me speak of another; this one was not a slave. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA). A man of the tribe of Ghifar; they carried no special weight with Makkah. He had come to Makkah in search of the truth. He met the Prophet {{1}}, and accepted Islam at once.
blocks.37: The Prophet {{1}} told him, now go back to your tribe. Do not say this openly. Abu Dharr (RA) did not listen. He went straight to al-Masjid al-Haram, stood in the midst of the crowd, raised his voice and said, I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.
blocks.38: The Quraysh pounced. Beating him, they threw him to the ground. ‘Abbas came and bent over him. He said, what are you doing! This is a man of Ghifar; the trade route to Sham is in their hands. Let him go.{{1}}
blocks.39: The next day Abu Dharr (RA) did the same thing again. Was beaten again. Again ‘Abbas saved him. No one forced him. Hiding would have been enough. But the thing he had found did not seem to him something to keep behind a closed mouth.
blocks.40: Today we often walk the opposite way. Even the little that cannot but be said we swallow; lest someone think something. For Abu Dharr (RA) the din was such a thing that one who finds it cannot stay silent.
blocks.42: After all we have heard, one question is natural. Could Allah not have stopped all this! He could. In one moment He could. Then why did He let it happen! The answer is in the Qur’an itself
blocks.44: Alif-Lam-Mim. Do people think that merely by saying ‘We have believed’ they will be left without being tested? Yet We tested those who passed before them as well. So Allah will surely find out who showed truthfulness, and He will surely find out who are the liars.{{1}}
blocks.45: There is a hard thing inside the verse. Saying ‘we have believed’ is no proof. Anyone can say it with the mouth. In easy times everyone says it. But what faith really is, that is known only when a price has to be paid for it.
blocks.46: The one who lies on the burning sand and says ‘Ahad’, his word is proven. The one who says it sitting in an air-conditioned room, his word has not yet been tested. Test does not mean punishment. Test means verification.
blocks.47: To verify gold it must be put in the fire. The fire is not the enemy of the gold; it is the enemy of the dross. There is another side. The test is not only verification; it is also forming. The ummah that is to lead the world has to be formed first.
blocks.48: What did Allah form in these thirteen years of Makkah! Some people who do not change their word even at the price of their lives. Later it was at the hands of these very people that Rome and Persia collapsed.
blocks.49: People formed in easy times can do easy work. For hard work, people formed in hard times are needed. So the hardship was not punishment. It was training.
blocks.51: There is another scene in the Qur’an; of those who believed before us. A kingdom. A tyrant king. And a group of people who had acknowledged the One Allah. The king had long trenches dug by the roadside. The trenches were filled with fire. Then it was announced; whoever will not give up faith will be thrown into this fire.
blocks.52: Not one stepped back. One by one they were thrown into that fire. And the king and his men sat at the edge of the pit and watched.
blocks.54: May Allah’s curse be on the people of the ditch, the people of the fire full of fuel. When they were sitting beside it and were watching what they were doing to the believers. They were punishing the believers only because they had believed in that Allah, who is possessed of great power, worthy of all praise.{{1}}
blocks.56: The last word of the verse is important here. ‘Only because they had believed in Allah.’ The offence was one. When a man steals he is punished, when he kills he is punished; that is understandable. But here the offence was belief.
blocks.57: In this one place Jahiliyyah is always the same. It can tolerate the thief, but it cannot tolerate the one who is unwilling to bow his head.
blocks.58: The Fire That Does Not Burn Gold
blocks.59: In the story of the People of the Ditch there is a thing not everyone notices. None of them survived. No angel came down. The fire did not turn cold. The king’s throne did not fall. All of them burned.
blocks.60: And Allah kept the story in the Qur’an. Right here an idea of ours needs breaking. We think, if faith is right, the trouble will pass. The illness will be cured. The job will come through.
blocks.61: But Allah has promised this nowhere. He has promised that He is watching. And keeping the account. Sumayyah (RA) did not survive. The people of the Ditch did not survive. Yet they are the ones who won. Because the definition of winning is not in our hands.
blocks.62: One more thing. We make du‘a, ‘O Allah, remove the trouble’. The du‘a is fine; we must make it. But another du‘a needs to be added alongside. ‘O Allah, if You do not remove the trouble, hold me firm.’
blocks.63: The first du‘a is about the situation. The second is about oneself. The situation does not always change. One can always be held firm.
blocks.65: In today’s dars we heard of a few people. Bilal, who had a rock on his chest and one word on his lips. Zinnirah, whose eyes were gone and whose argument was not. Sumayyah, who gave the first blood. ‘Ammar, who said it with his mouth and yet held his heart. Khabbab, whose back-scars stayed until death. Suhayb, who gave the savings of a whole life in one sentence.
blocks.66: Not one of them was a big man then. Slave, slave-woman, outsider, blacksmith. Those whose names were not in the ledger of Makkah. And today! No one names a son Abu Jahl. No one names a son Umayyah. No one names a son al-‘As ibn Wa’il.
blocks.67: But in millions of homes of the world even today sons are named Bilal. ‘Ammar. Khabbab. Suhayb. The names of those who beat have been wiped out. The names of those who were beaten remain.
blocks.68: This is Allah’s reckoning. And there is one more thing. None of them knew that their names would remain. Bilal (RA), lying on the sand, did not think that fourteen hundred years later in some home in Bangladesh a boy would be born with my name.
blocks.69: He only held on to one word. The rest Allah did. In the coming dars we shall see what happened when this persecution went beyond endurance; the first Hijrah, to Abyssinia, and the acceptance of Islam in Makkah by two men, which changed the whole reckoning.
blocks.70: So take one task from today’s dars. From now on speak of your hardship not in gatherings but on the prayer mat. Ya‘qub (AS) laid his grief and sorrow before Allah right there.
blocks.72: Under Bilal’s (RA) back, scorching sand; on his chest, a rock. On his lips one word only; Ahad. Today I will ask myself one question: what price have I paid for my kalimah?
blocks.73: From today I will speak of hardship not to people but on the prayer mat, which from today I will not give up.

As for the scene “‘Umar (RA) seated him beside himself and said, only one man is worthy of this seat; then Khabbab (RA) uncovered his back and showed the scars”, it is the narration of Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 3/116–118 and al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; there is discussion about the chain. This part is used as a scene, not as proof.
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1276 and 4047; from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA). Verified on hadithunlocked.com (bukhari:1276). Concerning the difficulty of the shroud of Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA) and the saying ‘the fruit of some of us has ripened, he is gathering it’.
footnotes.3: The Companionship of Suhayb ibn Sinan (RA) and his standing are established by sound chains. The incident belongs to the Hijrah period; here it is brought briefly only by way of introducing Suhayb (RA), with details in the dars on the Hijrah.
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3522; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2474. The acceptance of Islam by Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA), the advice of the Prophet {{1}} to him to keep it secret, his giving open testimony of the kalimah in al-Masjid al-Haram, the beating by the Quraysh, the same incident again the next day, and the intervention of ‘Abbas; all are narrated by sound chains in this long hadith.
footnotes.7: The detailed account of the People of the Ditch comes in Sahih Muslim, hadith 3005 (the long hadith of the boy, the monk and the sorcerer). It should be noted that in the note of Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an it is said that the narration of Muslim does not state explicitly that the people of the ditch in Surah al-Buruj are the people of this very incident; this link was made by Muhammad ibn Ishaq (RH). So the statement of the verse is definitive, while the detailed form of the incident is report-based.

quiz.q: In the shade of the Ka‘bah, what did Khabbab (RA) ask of the Prophet ﷺ?
o: Permission to leave Makkah
Permission to fight the Quraysh
Du‘a and help for us
Permission to carry on deeds in secret
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ was then sitting reclined on his cloak. He sat up, his face turned red, and he spoke of the persecution of earlier communities.

quiz.q: What persecution of earlier believers did the Prophet ﷺ mention?
o: Drowned in the sea, and houses all burned
Placed in a pit and split with a saw, flesh stripped with iron combs
Driven from the city and all wealth seized
Paraded in the market, humiliated and imprisoned
quiz.e: Yet they would not turn from the din. With it he said, this work will be completed; a rider will go from San‘a to Hadramawt, with no fear of anyone but Allah.

quiz.q: What was the reason for the face of the Prophet ﷺ turning red in the shade of the Ka‘bah?
o: The insolence of Khabbab (RA)
Hearing news of fresh oppression by the Quraysh
The idea ‘if you follow the din there will be no hardship’
Seeing the impatience of the Companions
quiz.e: He broke that very idea. In the same breath he said two things; there will be hardship on this path, and this will surely be completed.

quiz.q: When du‘a seems to bring no result, which point does the dars recall?
o: The words of the du‘a must be changed
More sadaqah must be given
Allah’s clock is not our clock
Du‘a must be dropped and effort begun
quiz.e: Khabbab (RA) got what he asked for, but not at once. A foundation laid in haste, nothing stands on it.

quiz.q: What did the dars mean by the analogy ‘the child asks today, the father gives tomorrow’?
o: There can be good even behind the delay
Merely a method of teaching patience
Teaching the right manner of asking
Explaining the child’s right over the father
quiz.e: The boy thinks the father did not give; the father knows that giving today would have harmed him. The difference is, the father’s knowledge is limited, while the One we ask has infinite knowledge.

quiz.q: What problem arose with the shroud of Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA)?
o: No cloth could be found that day
None of the Companions came forward to shroud him
The cloth was so costly it could not be used
Covering the head with one cloak left the feet out
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, cover the head and put idhkhir grass over the feet. Khabbab (RA) would weep telling this incident.

quiz.q: Why did Khabbab (RA) weep after becoming well off?
o: Remembering the hardships of old days again and again
Whether he had received his reward in this world itself
Out of fear of losing his wealth
Feeling the absence of old companions
quiz.e: We fear, why did I get nothing in this world. He feared, why did I get in this world. The whole difference lies between the two fears.

quiz.q: What does the dars say about measuring Allah’s love by wealth or want?
o: Having wealth is proof of Allah’s love
Having want is proof of Allah’s displeasure
Both are tests; the question is what I did
Keeping wealth is itself the fault
quiz.e: The one who has nothing thinks Allah has forgotten him, the one who has everything thinks Allah loves him; both are wrong reckonings.

quiz.q: What did Suhayb ibn Sinan (RA) do at the time of the Hijrah?
o: Slipped out secretly in the dark of night
Gave up all his wealth and got the way
Made a treaty with the Quraysh
Mingled with a caravan
quiz.e: The Quraysh blocked the way and said, you came penniless, built wealth, and now will take it all! He gave everything. The Prophet ﷺ said, the deal was profitable, O Abu Yahya!

quiz.q: Despite the advice of the Prophet ﷺ to keep it secret, what did Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) do?
o: Openly testified to the kalimah before the Ka‘bah
Quietly returned to his tribe
Went to the houses of the Quraysh leaders and called them in secret
Migrated to Abyssinia
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ had asked him to keep it secret; Abu Dharr (RA) raised his voice in al-Masjid al-Haram amid the crowd and testified, was beaten for two days, and ‘Abbas saved him.

quiz.q: According to Surah al-‘Ankabut, why is merely saying ‘we have believed’ not enough?
o: Faith shows itself only in action
The words must be said in Arabic
Because no one’s word is acceptable without witnesses
The word of the mouth can be said by anyone in easy times
quiz.e: What faith is, is known only when a price has to be paid for it. Test is not punishment, it is verification; the fire is not the enemy of gold, it is the enemy of the dross.

quiz.q: According to Surah al-Buruj, what was the ‘offence’ of the believers of the ditch?
o: They had directly disobeyed the king’s order
Only believing in Allah
They had organised in secret
They had opposed the sorcerer
quiz.e: The words of the verse: ‘only because they had believed in Allah’. Jahiliyyah tolerates the thief, but cannot tolerate the one who does not bow his head.

quiz.q: If the trouble does not pass, which additional du‘a does the dars ask us to add?
o: Cursing the enemy
Hold me firm even if You do not remove it
Praying for a quick solution
Having someone else make du‘a
quiz.e: The first du‘a is about the situation, the second about oneself. The situation does not always change; one can always be held firm.

quiz.q: What is the practical resolve of this dars?
o: Reading one page of the Sirah daily
Giving a little sadaqah at least daily
Not missing the prayers I skip out of laziness
Memorising the names of the persecuted Companions
quiz.e: The first demand of the kalimah that Bilal (RA) held on to with a rock on his chest is prayer.

quiz.q: What is the biggest lesson from the names of those who beat being wiped out?
o: Allah’s reckoning is exact, even if late
The tyrant is always destroyed quickly
Learning the rules for naming children
History tells only of the victors
quiz.e: Today in millions of homes sons are named Bilal, ‘Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb; no one names a son Abu Jahl or Umayyah. None of them knew their names would remain.
